questions.question: Surah Ar-Rahman is traditionally known as the 'Bride of the Quran' due to its extraordinary beauty and its recurring divine refrain.
questions.explanation: Classical scholars titled Surah Ar-Rahman 'Arous al-Quran' (Bride of the Quran) because of its lyrical beauty, rhythmic structure, and the powerful recurring challenge — 'Then which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?' — that runs through it 31 times.

questions.question: Why does the surah mention the teaching of the Quran before the creation of humanity in verses 2-3?
options: A. To indicate that jinn received the Quran before humans did
B. To show that divine guidance was decreed as a prior act of mercy before Adam was even formed
C. To suggest that prophets were created alongside the Quran
D. To emphasize that only scholars can access the Quran's full meaning
questions.explanation: Placing Quran-teaching before human creation signals that Allah's mercy in providing guidance was planned and decreed before mankind came into existence — establishing divine generosity as the very foundation of this surah's opening.

questions.question: What does 'al-bayan' refer to in verse 4, where Allah states He taught humanity 'al-bayan'?
options: A. The ability to write and record scripture
B. Mathematical reasoning and logical thought
C. Eloquent speech and the power of clear, articulate expression
D. The capacity to hear divine revelation directly
questions.explanation: Al-bayan in verse 4 refers to the gift of eloquent, articulate expression — the uniquely human capacity to communicate meaning clearly. This gift is listed alongside the teaching of the Quran as one of Allah's supreme favors in the surah's opening.

questions.question: Verse 7 of Surah Ar-Rahman addresses both the elevation of the heavens and the establishment of the balance (mizan) in a single verse, linking cosmic order with moral obligation.
questions.explanation: In verse 7, Allah mentions raising the heaven and setting up the mizan (balance) together, presenting cosmic structure and ethical law as two expressions of the same divine design — the physical universe and justice are inseparable in this surah's worldview.

questions.question: How many times does the refrain 'Then which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?' appear in Surah Ar-Rahman?
options: A. 7 times
B. 21 times
C. 31 times
D. 99 times
questions.explanation: The divine refrain is repeated exactly 31 times throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, addressing both mankind and jinn. It punctuates each description of Allah's favors as a rhythmic challenge, building an overwhelming cumulative case against ingratitude.

questions.question: The phrase 'salsaal kal-fakhkhar' used to describe the creation of man in verse 14 means what?
options: A. Fragrant clay mixed with water
B. Sounding clay like pottery — clay that rings when struck
C. Soft mud dried by the sun
D. Black altered mud from riverbanks
questions.explanation: Salsaal kal-fakhkhar describes clay that produces a ringing sound when struck, like fired pottery or ceramic. This vivid description captures a specific stage in the creation of the human body before Allah breathed His spirit into it.

questions.question: According to verse 15, jinn were created from smokeless fire, which classical scholars consistently distinguish from the clay associated with the origin of human beings.
questions.explanation: Verse 15 specifies 'marij min naar' — a smokeless, intensely hot flame — as the substance from which jinn were created. Classical commentators note this clearly distinguishes jinn's origin from Adam's clay, establishing the two beings as categorically different creations.

questions.question: Imam al-Tabari's grammatical analysis holds that 'Ar-Rahman' in verse 1 functions as which part of the sentence in relation to 'taught the Quran' in verse 2?
options: A. An object, with verse 2 as an active participle
B. The subject (mubtada), with verse 2 serving as the predicate (khabar)
C. A vocative address to the Prophet
D. An appositive modifying a divine name mentioned earlier
questions.explanation: Al-Tabari analyzed 'Ar-Rahman' as the grammatical subject (mubtada) and 'taught the Quran' as its predicate (khabar), producing the declaration: 'The Most Merciful — He taught the Quran.' This grounds the Quran's very existence in divine mercy.

questions.question: Ibn Kathir, commenting on verse 5, explains that the sun and moon run by a precise divine reckoning such that neither overtakes the other nor deviates from its appointed course.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir's tafsir on verse 5 ('the sun and moon run by precise calculation') emphasizes that husban denotes a fixed divine reckoning by which both celestial bodies travel without collision or deviation — one of the grand cosmic signs of Allah's power listed in the surah.

questions.question: A hadith recorded by Imam al-Tirmidhi describes the Prophet reciting Surah Ar-Rahman to his Companions and then to a group of jinn. Which group responded more readily to the refrain?
options: A. The Companions, who immediately declared none of Allah's favors they would deny
B. Both groups responded with equal enthusiasm
C. The jinn, who declared none of Allah's favors they would deny at each repetition of the refrain
D. Neither group responded — silence was considered the correct response
questions.explanation: The Tirmidhi hadith reports that when the Prophet recited Surah Ar-Rahman to the jinn, they responded to each refrain by declaring 'None of Your favors, O Lord, do we deny.' The Prophet then told the Companions that the jinn had given a better response than they had — making this response the intended model of acknowledgment.

questions.question: A hadith in Sahih Muslim states that angels were created from light, jinn from fire, and Adam from what was described to us — directly paralleling the distinctions made in verses 14-15 of this surah.
questions.explanation: The Prophet said, as recorded in Sahih Muslim: 'The angels were created from light, the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you.' This hadith confirms and grounds the Quranic account of diverse creation in verses 14-15.

questions.question: Ibn Kathir, in his commentary on verse 60 ('Is the reward for ihsan anything but ihsan?'), identifies what as the ultimate recompense for those who worship Allah with excellence?
options: A. Forgiveness of all sins without any accountability on the Day of Judgment
B. A rank above the angels in the hereafter
C. Ihsan in return — excellence met with excellence, embodied in the gift of Paradise
D. A worldly reward in the form of increased provision and honor
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir explains that verse 60 establishes a divine principle: the reward for ihsan (excellence in worship and conduct) is ihsan from Allah in return — Paradise itself being the supreme form of divine generosity that mirrors and surpasses the excellence of the servant.

questions.question: Muhammad al-Sha'rawi argued that the sky's elevation mentioned in verse 7 symbolically bears witness against those who violate the scales of justice on earth.
questions.explanation: Al-Sha'rawi connected the celestial order of verse 7 to moral obligation: just as the heavens are held in perfect balance by divine will, the mizan on earth must be honored by human beings — the elevated sky stands as a cosmic witness against those who cheat in measure and weight.

questions.question: Wahbah al-Zuhayli, in his commentary on verse 46, connects fearing the 'station of one's Lord' (khafa maqama rabbihi) to which spiritual concept in Islamic ethics?
options: A. Tawbah — repentance performed after committing a sin
B. Muraqabah — continuous God-consciousness, worshipping as if Allah watches at every moment
C. Zuhd — complete renunciation of worldly pleasures and possessions
D. Tawakkul — absolute reliance on Allah that excludes personal effort
questions.explanation: Al-Zuhayli connects 'khafa maqama rabbihi' in verse 46 to muraqabah — the state of continuous God-consciousness in which a believer acts as if Allah observes them at every moment. This is the spiritual engine behind the Quran's promise of two paradises for those who cultivate this awareness.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, describes the paradise imagery beginning from verse 48 as functioning like what kind of experience for the believing reader?
options: A. A legal contract specifying the precise entitlements of the righteous
B. A historical account of gardens given to prophets in this world
C. A sensory revelation that lets the heart taste paradise before arriving there
D. An allegory with no literal meaning, pointing only to inner spiritual peace
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb writes in Fi Zilal that the vivid sensory descriptions of paradise in Ar-Rahman function as a 'sensory revelation' — drawing the reader's heart into a direct, felt encounter with divine beauty so that faith is kindled through longing and imagination, not merely rational reflection.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb argues that specifying the lining of the paradise couches in verse 54 implies that the outer side of these couches surpasses anything found in this world.
questions.explanation: Qutb observes that Allah mentions the inner lining of the couches — brocade — to hint that if the hidden inner side is this magnificent, the outer side transcends description entirely. This rhetorical move underscores that paradise's beauty cannot be captured by any worldly comparison.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, gives verse 60 — 'Is the reward for ihsan anything but ihsan?' — a specific title. What does he call it?
options: A. The retributive principle of equal punishment for equal sin
B. A legal formula for calculating reward based on deeds recorded by the angels
C. 'The great principle' — a universal moral law that excellence is always met with excellence
D. An abrogated verse whose meaning was clarified by later Medinan revelation
questions.explanation: Qutb calls verse 60 'al-qa'ida al-kubra' (the great principle) in Fi Zilal, presenting it as a universal divine law: wherever there is genuine excellence — in worship, character, or human relations — Allah responds with excellence. It is not merely a transactional promise but a cosmic moral truth.

questions.question: The phrase 'min doonihima' (below or beneath those two) in verse 62, which introduces the second pair of paradises, is understood by contemporary Sunni scholars to establish what?
options: A. That the lower paradises are reserved exclusively for non-Muslims who lived righteously
B. A graduated hierarchy of paradise in which spiritual merit determines the degree of reward
C. That the second pair of gardens exists in a different universe from the first pair
D. That the second two paradises are allegorical only and have no real existence
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli and other contemporary Sunni scholars understand 'min doonihima' as establishing a graduated hierarchy within paradise: the higher two gardens (verses 46-61) belong to those who attained the loftiest spiritual station, while the second pair (verses 62-77) represents a slightly lower — yet still magnificent — degree, with a believer's spiritual merit determining which level they enter.
